title: Nepal Premier League: Pokhara Avengers Secure First Win, Kathmandu Gurkhas Top Standings - Ratopati
description: Nepal Premier League: Pokhara Avengers Secure First Win, Kathmandu Gurkhas Top Standings  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. The two matches played on Monday under the third edition of the Nepal Premier League (NPL) have made the points table equation more interesting.

Pokhara Avengers, under pressure after losing four consecutive matches, secured their first win in the tournament by defeating Karnali Yaks by a wide margin. Meanwhile, Kathmandu Gurkhas climbed to the top of the points table by defeating Chitwan Rhinos.

In the first match on Monday, Pokhara defeated Karnali by 63 runs, and in the second match, Kathmandu registered a 10-run victory over Chitwan. These results, on one hand, keep Pokhara's playoff hopes alive, and on the other hand, strengthen Kathmandu's claim.

Under pressure after suffering four consecutive defeats, Pokhara displayed an excellent performance in both batting and bowling against Karnali on Monday. Batting first after losing the toss, Pokhara scored 217 runs for the loss of 3 wickets in the stipulated 20 overs.

For Pokhara, Yuvraj Samra played an excellent century innings of 102 runs off 48 balls, with 6 sixes and 10 fours. His century in the NPL became a significant achievement for Pokhara. Kushal Bhurtel, who supported him, scored 62 runs off 39 balls with 7 sixes. The aggressive batting between these two led Pokhara towards a huge total.

Towards the end, captain Chamika Karunaratne remained unbeaten on 35 off 11 balls, with 3 sixes and 3 fours, enabling Pokhara to achieve a strong total of 217 runs. Karnali's captain Sompal Kami took 2 wickets, and Mark Watt took 1 wicket. However, Karnali's bowlers failed to stop Pokhara's batsmen from scoring big.

Pokhara's 217 runs is the second-highest team total in NPL history. Earlier, in the second edition, Biratnagar Kings had scored 220 runs against Pokhara. This shows how impressive Pokhara's batting performance was. Chasing a huge target of 218 runs, Karnali could only manage 154 runs for all out in 18.3 overs. For Karnali, Pawan Sarraf scored 32 off 31 balls, Ariful Islam scored 24 off 13 balls, and Dipak Dumre scored 22 off 7 balls, but they couldn't lead the team to victory.

Pokhara's Mehdi Hasan took 3 wickets. Dhananjaya Lakshan, Kushal Bhurtel, and Bipin Khatri took 2 wickets each, causing Karnali's innings to collapse. The manner of dismissal of Karnali captain Sompal Kami in this match also garnered special attention. He hit the ball again with his bat after hitting it with the bat off Mehdi Hasan's ball. The umpire then reviewed the video and declared him out on the basis of 'Obstructing the Field'. In cricket, this rule can be attracted if a batsman intentionally hits the ball a second time in a way that affects the play.

This victory has brought great relief to Pokhara, which was winless for four matches. The team has opened its account on the points table for the first time. On the other hand, Karnali, with 4 points from five matches, has dropped to seventh place. Karnali's playoff journey is also becoming difficult due to consecutive losses.

Reacting after the match, centurion Yuvraj Samra said that he was able to score big runs by trying to take the game lightly. According to him, the plan was to put pressure on the opposition bowlers from the beginning and perform well in the powerplay. He said that although he couldn't play according to his plan in the previous match, he succeeded in his strategy this time. His strategy was to play aggressive shots when the ball was hittable and take one or two runs to change strike if that was not the case.

Expressing happiness at being able to play in front of the Nepali audience after coming to Nepal from Canada, he mentioned that the audience's support gave him more enthusiasm. He also said that his experience playing in the T-20 World Cup and various franchise leagues has helped improve his game.

Yuvraj dedicated his century and the team's victory to his parents. He also praised the performance of Pokhara's bowlers, saying they made good use of the grip and turn from the pitch.

After the defeat, Karnali's batsman Pawan Sarraf said that losing wickets continuously in the powerplay was the main reason for the defeat. According to him, if a good partnership had been formed at the beginning, there would have been a possibility of chasing the target set by Pokhara. However, he said that after losing wickets at the start, the middle-order batsmen also came under pressure.

Pawan admitted that although Karnali performed well at the start of the tournament, they could not maintain their rhythm in the recent matches. He also mentioned weaknesses in fielding along with batting. He stated that despite losing three consecutive matches, the playoff chances were not over, and they had to win both remaining matches.

Kathmandu in the Top Spot

In the second match on Monday, Kathmandu Gurkhas defeated Chitwan Rhinos by 10 runs. Batting first, Kathmandu scored 180 runs for the loss of 8 wickets in the stipulated 20 overs. For Kathmandu, the batsman who scored 52 runs off 28 balls with 4 sixes and 2 fours performed excellently. Similarly, Sahaj Rachige scored 33 off 20 balls, William Bosisto scored 27 off 22 balls, and captain Karan KC scored 20 off 7 balls. For Chitwan, Rijan Dhakal bowled excellently, conceding 14 runs and taking 3 wickets in 4 overs. Sikandar Raza and Kamal Airee took 2 wickets each, and Don Maousley took 1 wicket.

Chasing a target of 181 runs, Chitwan could only manage 170 runs for the loss of 7 wickets in the stipulated 20 overs. For Chitwan, Ravi Bopara played a half-century innings of 55 runs off 35 balls with 3 sixes and 2 fours. Don Maousley scored 29, Kamil Mishara scored 28, and Arjun Saud scored 23.

However, Chitwan could not reach the target as the middle and lower-order batsmen failed to score at the required pace. For Kathmandu, Sahaj Rachige took 2 wickets, while captain Karan KC, Jahandad Khan, Santosh Yadav, and Ganesh Gautam took 1 wicket each.

With this victory, Kathmandu climbed to the top of the points table with 8 points from five matches. After losing the first match, Kathmandu has shown excellent form by winning four consecutive matches. Chitwan, after the defeat, remains in fourth place.

After the victory against Chitwan, Kathmandu's director Sharad Vesawkar attributed the success mainly to the team's balance and coordination among the players. According to him, a plan was made during the auction to keep backup players ready. He said that the team was built in such a way that if any player got injured, another player could easily take responsibility.

He also praised the performance of young player Ganesh Gautam, who got an opportunity in place of the injured Sahab Alam. He said that Ganesh, who was selected from about 500 players through talent hunt, performed well in his first match. Coach Vesawkar also stated that the arrival of experienced Australian batsman David Warner in Kathmandu has benefited the team. He mentioned that the team has won all four matches played since Warner's arrival, and Warner's experience and on-field advice have helped the players.

After the defeat, Chitwan's experienced player Ravi Bopara said that they had to face defeat due to losing wickets continuously despite being in a good position.

According to him, Chitwan had lost only one wicket for 85 runs in 10 overs. He said that at that time, the team was in a position to win, and the pitch was also good for batting. However, he said that they could not keep the game in their favor due to losing wickets continuously thereafter.

Bopara also said that the power-hitting ability of Nepali batsmen has improved significantly in the last two years. He opined that although Nepali players have improved their ability to play big shots, foreign players also have to take responsibility for the defeat.

He praised the performance of Chitwan's bowlers Rijan Dhakal and Kamal Singh Airee. Stating that the upcoming match against Pokhara is very important for Chitwan, he mentioned that they have to win that match.

Both matches on Monday have made the NPL playoff race more competitive. While Kathmandu, with 8 points from five matches, has climbed to the top spot, Pokhara, after losing four consecutive matches, has shown signs of a comeback by securing its first win.

For Chitwan and Karnali, the results of the remaining matches will be very important. Especially Karnali, after reaching seventh place with 4 points from five matches, is under pressure to win the upcoming matches.

Pokhara's first win has boosted their confidence. The century by Yuvraj Samra, aggressive batting by Kushal Bhurtel, and effective performance by the bowlers have added new energy to the team.

Overall, in Monday's matches, Pokhara has proven its batting prowess and shown signs of returning to the competition, while Kathmandu has maintained its winning streak and strengthened its claim for the title. The final equation of the playoffs will be determined by the performance of these teams in the remaining matches.

title: Indian anti-dumping duties put Nepal’s jute industry under pressure - The Kathmandu Post
description: Indian anti-dumping duties put Nepal’s jute industry under pressure  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
India is the biggest market for jute products manufactured in Nepal. But Nepali manufacturers now face higher charges to sell their products in the very market on which they depend most.

India’s decision to increase anti-dumping duties on Nepali jute products has added to the pressure on the industry, particularly in eastern Nepal, where most of the country’s jute mills are based.

Anti-dumping duties are additional tariffs imposed to protect a country’s domestic industries from imports sold at prices below their normal market value or production costs. Such duties can be levied when a foreign company is found to be selling goods at artificially low prices to gain an unfair advantage in another country’s market. This practice is known as dumping.

India has increased the duties on Nepali jute products under this provision. According to a notification issued by India's Ministry of Finance on September 24, 2026, anti-dumping duties on hessian fabric, jute bags and jute yarn and twine have been set at different rates depending on the product and manufacturer.

The revised rates are about four times higher than those previously imposed on some Nepali manufacturers. Swastik Jute Mills in Biratnagar, for instance, previously paid $8.18 per tonne in anti-dumping duties on hessian fabric exported to India. Under the new arrangement, the rate has risen to $132 per tonne. Similarly, the duty on hessian fabric exported by Baba Jute Mills has increased from $6.30 to $64 per tonne.

For some manufacturers, however, countervailing duties are higher than anti-dumping duties. Countervailing duties are additional tariffs imposed to offset the impact of subsidies provided by a foreign government to its domestic industries, which may give exporters an unfair advantage over producers in the importing country.

India’s Directorate General of Trade Remedies (DGTR) has recommended countervailing duties ranging from $54.77 to $60.54 per tonne on jute products imported from Nepal. India began the process of imposing such duties on jute products imported from Nepal and Bangladesh in 2025.

Rajkumar Golchha, president of the Nepal Jute Industries Association, said the industry had repeatedly drawn the government’s attention to the anti-dumping duties.

“We expect this issue to be discussed seriously during the prime minister’s upcoming visit to India,” Golchha said. “There is little possibility of resolving the problem without an understanding between the two governments.”

Nepal accounts for less than 1 percent of India’s total jute production. Golchha argues that Nepali manufacturers cannot realistically be accused of undercutting Indian producers, as they depend on India and Bangladesh for raw materials and spare parts.

Golchha, who also runs two of Nepal’s major jute manufacturers, Raghupati Jute Mills and Arihant Multifibres, said India had initiated trade remedy proceedings based on the impact of imports on its domestic industry and the effects of subsidies provided by foreign governments.

Anti-dumping and countervailing duties are two distinct trade measures. The former seeks to protect domestic industries from imports sold at unfairly low prices, while the latter addresses the effects of subsidies provided by foreign governments.

Nepal’s jute industry exports products worth around Rs11 billion annually. Exports of jute products reached Rs10.89 billion in the last fiscal year, with hessian fabric shipments to India accounting for the largest share.

In the last fiscal year, Nepal exported hessian fabric worth Rs7.2681 billion to India. Exports of jute bags exceeded Rs2.74 billion, while those of ropes amounted to around Rs880 million.

The figures underline the industry’s heavy dependence on the Indian market. With duties rising, Nepali manufacturers may have to increase the prices of their products in India or absorb the additional costs themselves. Raising prices could make their products less competitive, while absorbing the duties would increase production costs and squeeze profit margins.

According to Golchha, the prospects for exporting Nepali jute products to third-country markets are also limited. Nepal is farther from seaports than India and Bangladesh, making transportation more expensive. Finding an alternative to the Indian market in the short term would therefore be difficult.

The industry is also losing export incentives previously provided by the Nepali government. A 4 percent export subsidy on jute products is no longer available. Golchha said the facility had been suspended for around a year and a half.

With export duties rising in India and government support withdrawn at home, Nepali manufacturers face mounting pressure on both production costs and their ability to compete in the international market.

The jute industry is not merely an industrial activity in eastern Nepal; it is also closely linked to agriculture and employment. Jute is cultivated in districts including Jhapa, Morang and Sunsari, involving around 100,000 farmers. Farmers and workers are engaged in various stages of the supply chain, from cultivation and processing to retting, washing and packaging.

Golchha said Nepal’s jute industry currently employs between 10,000 and 14,000 workers directly, more than half of whom are women. A prolonged crisis in the sector could therefore affect not only factory workers but also farmers and labourers involved in cultivation and processing.

According to Golchha, 12 jute mills were operating in the Morang-Sunsari area until recently. Only six are now in operation.

Industry representatives have urged the Nepali government to pursue high-level diplomatic efforts to persuade India to reconsider the increased duties. Golchha said the government should give the jute industry the same priority it had given to resolving problems faced by the tea industry.

Representatives of business organisations in Morang have also called on the government to intervene diplomatically to prevent India from imposing anti-dumping duties on Nepali jute products at rates up to four times higher than the existing ones from October.

A delegation from the Morang Industry Organisation met Industry, Commerce and Supplies Minister Deepak Kumar Sah on September 27 and urged him to initiate diplomatic efforts.

“The government must raise the issue firmly through diplomatic channels and work towards the complete removal of anti-dumping duties,” said Nanda Kishor Rathi, president of the Morang Industry Organisation.

title: Nepal Calls for Just Energy Transition at COP-31 - Ratopati
description: Nepal Calls for Just Energy Transition at COP-31  Ratopati
publisher.title: Ratopati
full_article:
Kathmandu. A just energy transition has been demanded for countries dependent on fuel imports.

Speakers at an event organized at the Nepal Pavilion during the 31st Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP-31) in Antalya, Turkey, emphasized the need for international grant-based and accessible climate finance.

At the event titled 'From the Himalayas to the World: Roadmaps for a Just Transition from Fossil Fuels for Vulnerable Economies' under COP-31, Deputy Secretary of the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment of Nepal, Dr. Prakash Singh Thapa, presented his views.

In his presentation, Dr. Thapa stated that the transition to clean energy should not leave behind economically and socially vulnerable communities, workers, and climate-vulnerable countries.

He mentioned that although Nepal contributes less than 0.1 percent to global greenhouse gas emissions, it faces significant risks from melting glaciers, flash floods, landslides, and other climate-related disasters.

His statement indicated that Nepal's economy, particularly the agriculture, eco-tourism, construction, and forest sectors, are being affected by climate change, and the livelihoods of workers in these sectors are also at risk.

He presented the damage to life and property and the impact on hydropower infrastructure caused by the Bhote Koshi flood on August 26 as an example of climate risk.

The presentation estimated that 14 hydropower projects were damaged by the disaster, and approximately US$4.7 billion would be required for reconstruction and rehabilitation.

Deputy Secretary Dr. Thapa informed that Nepal has committed to achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2045 and aims to reach 28,500 megawatts of renewable energy capacity by 2035.

He further stated that implementing Nepal's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) requires US$73.74 billion for emission reduction by 2035, of which 85 percent, or US$62.92 billion, needs to be mobilized through international cooperation.

He highlighted that Nepal's need to import petroleum products and most coal creates a significant financial burden on the economy, emphasizing the need to reduce fuel import dependency through the expansion of clean energy production and consumption.

A just transition is not merely a process of moving from fossil fuels to renewable energy but also a process that ensures employment, social security, decent work, gender equality, and economic rights for affected workers and communities.

Nepal views COP-31 as an opportunity to implement international commitments related to just transition, ensure climate finance, and establish the concerns of climate-vulnerable countries in global climate negotiations.

In the group discussions held on the occasion, speakers emphasized the need for a just transition from fossil fuel-based economies to clean energy, considering the needs and conditions of economically vulnerable countries most at risk from the impacts of climate change.

The participating speakers expressed the view that the energy transition should be addressed not just as an environmental issue but as an economic, social, and development matter.

They shared their views on the need to balance clean energy promotion, economic development, and climate justice for climate-vulnerable countries like Nepal.

Executive Director of Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative Alex Rafalowicz, Executive Director of NGO Forum Cambodia Soeung Saroun, Executive Director of World Youth Climate Justice Jules Schanckenberg, Director of Stamp Out Poverty David Hillman, and Senior Legal Advisor at the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL) Erika Lennon presented their views on the subject.

The event discussed the economic and social challenges faced by developing countries in the process of gradually reducing fossil fuel use and expanding clean and renewable energy, the required investment, international cooperation, and policy aspects of a just transition.

Addressing the potential impacts on workers, communities, and economies dependent on the transition from fossil fuels to clean energy is equally important.

The importance of international cooperation was highlighted at the event, as the burden of energy transition could fall on countries and communities with weak economies without adequate financial and technical support.

In the context of Nepal, utilizing the potential of hydropower, solar, and other renewable energy sources to expand clean energy production and consumption can be a significant basis for energy transition.

Himalayan countries like Nepal, which have contributed minimally to climate change, are facing significant climate-related disasters and environmental risks.

In this situation, it has been pointed out that international efforts for energy transition should address climate justice, equality, and the specific circumstances of developing countries.

The event provided an opportunity to present the common concerns of developing and vulnerable countries to the international forum by linking the climate challenges of the Himalayan region with global energy transition and climate justice debates.

title: President issues messages of best wishes on Nepal Sambat New Year 1147 - The Rising Nepal
description: President issues messages of best wishes on Nepal Sambat New Year 1147  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Nov 10: President Ramchandra Paudel has said that the Nepal Sambat, established by national figure Shankhadhar Sakhwa, is considered Nepal's indigenous calendar.

On the occasion of the Nepal Sambat New Year 1147, the President issued a message of best wishes today and recalled that this calendar was introduced in memory of Shankhadhar starting a new era by freeing the farmers and poor people in the Kathmandu Valley during the time of Lichhavi King Raghavdev.

President Paudel mentioned that in the context of Nepali society being civilized, tolerant, and united, such traditions have strengthened Nepali culture, history, independence, and identity.

The President mentioned that in Kathmandu Valley and various other parts of the country, this day is celebrated as a special festival marking the start of the new year, and reminded people of national figure Sakhuwa's efforts for people's freedom and economic liberation, which were welfare-oriented and philanthropic works.

The Head-of-State expressed his belief that today's day inspires everyone to stay selflessly committed and proactive for social equality, good governance, development, and progress.

President Paudel has wished that the Nepali calendar (Nepal Sambat) can help foster mutual harmony, tolerance, and a sense of fraternity among all Nepalis, strengthening the national unity.

The President has expressed the belief that the Nepal Sambat New Year will further help strengthen Nepal's independence, history, culture, and national identity.

Nepal Sambat calendar is symbol of social justice: Vice President Yadav

Similarly, in a message of best wishes he issued on the occasion of the Nepal Sambat New Year 1147, Vice President Ramsahay Prasad Yadav has said that the Nepal Sambat calendar is the living symbol of the originality of the Nepali civilization, liberalism, social justice and human co-existence.

The Vice President in his message said that the historic act by national figure Shankhadhar Sakhwa, who, driven by the spirit of public welfare, freed the suffering people from debt, has set a high standard of service, philanthropy, and social responsibility in Nepali society.

Vice President's message mentions that the humanitarian path shown by Sakhwa is still equally inspiring and exemplary for our national life today.

He has wished that this indigenous Nepali calendar fosters mutual trust, social harmony, cooperation, peace, and a spirit of working together among all Nepalis. (RSS)

Kathmandu, Nov 10: Chairperson of the National Assembly, Narayan Prasad Dahal, has said that festivals like Tihar, Nepal Sambat, and Chhath have been making an important contribution to strengthening national unity by promoting unity in diversity, tolerance, and mutual respect.

Wishing everyone on the occasions of Tihar, Nepal Sambat, Chhath, and various cultural festivals today, the Chairman of the upper house of the Federal Parliament has appealed to the general public to preserve indigenous culture and traditions and to promote environmentally friendly, respectful, and modest practices while celebrating these festivals.

Chairperson Dahal mentioned that Nepal's religions, culture, traditions, and festivals are invaluable national treasures, and the constitution of the Federal Democratic Republic of Nepal, achieved through the great struggle and sacrifices of the Nepali people, guarantees the protection of all religions, cultures, and traditions, as well as religious freedom.

He has wished that Tihar, Nepal Sambat, and Chhath festivals bring new enthusiasm, excitement, and positive energy to all Nepalis. (RSS)

title: Festivals foster social harmony, unity and tolerance: PM Shah - The Rising Nepal
description: Festivals foster social harmony, unity and tolerance: PM Shah  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Nov 10: Prime Minister Balendra Shah asserted that traditional festivals play an important role in bringing people together by encouraging them to set aside differences and fostering social unity, harmony and tolerance.

In a message marking Nepal Sambat 1147 (Nhu Daya Bhintuna) and Mha Puja, PM Shah extended warm greetings to Nepalis at home and abroad.

Describing Nepal Sambat as an integral part of the country's cultural identity and traditional lunar calendar, Shah recalled that national luminary Shankhadhar Sakhwa introduced the era after freeing people from debt.

He also highlighted the cultural and spiritual significance of Mha Puja, celebrated by the Newar community, saying the tradition promotes self-respect, self-awareness and spiritual purification.

''It also helps preserve ancestral heritage and foster harmony and solidarity within the community,'' the Head of the Government noted.

Similarly, Shah underscored the importance of Govardhan Puja and Goru Tihar, when oxen and agricultural tools are worshipped in recognition of their contribution to agriculture.

The celebrations are also associated with the Hindu belief that Lord Krishna lifted Govardhan Hill to protect the people of Dwarka.

He further observed that the traditional Bhailo and Deusi songs and blessings help strengthen neighbourhood ties and promote mutual goodwill.

The PM wished everyone happiness, peace, prosperity and progress on the festive occasions. (RSS)

title: Nepal Embassy in Delhi hosts Deusi-Bhailo celebrations as diaspora marks Tihar - WION
description: Nepal Embassy in Delhi hosts Deusi-Bhailo celebrations as diaspora marks Tihar  WION
publisher.title: WION
full_article:
Hundreds of members of Nepal’s community and diaspora gathered at the Embassy of Nepal in New Delhi to celebrate Deusi-Bhailo, the traditional folk singing and dancing that forms a central part of the Tihar festival. The event was led by Dr Surendra Thapa, Chargé d’Affaires in India. Speaking to WION, he said around 1,000 members of the Nepal diaspora were present. “The aim is to celebrate Nepali culture,” he noted, adding that “India and Nepal share culture.”

Also Read: Nepal eyes $2bn financial package, fresh air routes during PM Balen Shah's upcoming India visit

Deusi-Bhailo involves groups of men, women and children going from house to house during Tihar, singing traditional songs, dancing and offering blessings in exchange for gifts such as money, fruit or sel roti, a ring-shaped rice bread. Traditionally, Bhailo is performed by girls and women, often on the night of Laxmi Puja, while Deusi is sung by boys and men on the following nights, though mixed groups now commonly perform both. The practice is linked in folklore to the generosity of King Bali and is observed across Nepal as well as in Nepali communities in India and further afield.

The embassy’s programme continues its annual efforts to keep the tradition alive among Nepalis living in the Indian capital. Participants, many in traditional attire, performed the characteristic call-and-response songs and dances on the embassy grounds.

Also Read: Nepal Embassy in Delhi celebrates Kukur Tihar with garlands and tika for dogs

The gathering comes shortly after the embassy marked Kukur Tihar on 8 November. On that day, the second of the five-day Tihar festival, dogs were honoured with marigold garlands, red tika and special treats in recognition of their loyalty and companionship. Dr Thapa also led those celebrations, which were attended by members of the Nepali community, diplomats and embassy staff.

title: Nepal: Kathmandu Metropolitan City bans sale of plastic flowers - Floral Daily
description: Nepal: Kathmandu Metropolitan City bans sale of plastic flowers  Floral Daily
publisher.title: Floral Daily
full_article:
Kathmandu Metropolitan City has banned the sale of plastic flowers and decorative items. The Metropolitan Environment Management Department has issued a notice informing that the sale of plastic flowers and decorative items has been banned.

In addition, the metropolis has designated places for the sale of indigenous flowers in 33 locations within its geographical area. The Metropolitan Environment Management Department and the Metropolitan Police Force have published separate notices to publicize information related to such arrangements on the occasion of Diwali.

The Environment Management Department has stated in a notice, 'Using the authority granted by Section 15, Sub-section (6) of the Environment Protection Act, 2076 (2019), the Government of Nepal has completely banned the production, import, sale, distribution, or storage of plastic garlands and bouquets throughout Nepal. Furthermore, Kathmandu Metropolitan City has also completely banned the import, sale, distribution, or storage of plastic garlands and bouquets for many years.'

The notice states, 'Targeting the upcoming Tihar, we request all metropolitan residents to prioritize the sale and use of indigenous flowers and garlands by reducing the environmental damage caused by the use of imported plastic flower bouquets and garlands.'

title: Nepal Sambat common national inheritance of Nepalis: Speaker Aryal - The Rising Nepal
description: Nepal Sambat common national inheritance of Nepalis: Speaker Aryal  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Nov 10: Speaker Dol Prasad Aryal has reminded the struggle for Nepal Sambat is an important chapter in Nepal's democratic and cultural movement.

Addressing a programme organized by the Nhuda National Celebration Committee at Basantapur on the occasion of Nepal Sambat 1147 (New Year) today, Speaker Aryal further recalled that the movement for Nepal Sambat brought to light pressing voice for the rights of language, culture, script and identity in the party-less Panchayat system.

"Declaring Shankhadhar Sakhwa a national luminary, granting recognition to Nepal Sambat as a national calendar and the decision to include it in government documents are historic achievements of the movement," said Speaker Aryal, adding that it is essential to enforce these achievements in practice and amplify the use of Nepal Sambat in government offices, educational institutions and public bodies.

He said the Constitution of Nepal has finely recognized the multi-ethnic, multilingual and multicultural identity which is our national strength. "Nepal Sambat is a common national heritage of all Nepalis," Aryal argued.

Both the state and society should play their roles in protecting and promoting Nepal language, Ranjana script and the entire original cultural heritage, he stressed. Long-term protection will be possible if the new generation is made fully aware of this campaign, according to him.

"Nepal Sambat is not limited as a medium of calculating time, but a vital heritage of Nepal’s historical civilization, cultural pride and national identity", Speaker Aryal underscored.

The beginning of Nepal Sambat is linked to the contribution of national figure Shankhadhar Sakhwa, for he freed people from financial burden (debt) and gave a message of social justice, charity and collective welfare.

Also speaking on the occasion were Chief Minister of Bagmati Province, Kiran Thapamagar; federal Minister for Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation, Biraj Bhakta Shrestha; and acting mayor of Kathmandu Metropolitan City, Sunita Dangol. (RSS)

title: Pakistan demolish Nepal in Asia Cup - The Express Tribune
description: Pakistan demolish Nepal in Asia Cup  The Express Tribune
publisher.title: The Express Tribune
full_article:
Pakistan maintained their unbeaten run in the ACC Men’s Under-19 Asia Cup with a huge 101-run victory over Nepal in their final Group A match on Tuesday at the Al Amerat Cricket Ground in Oman.

The defending champions posted 275-7 in their allotted 50 overs before bowling Nepal out for 174 in 43.4 overs to register a comprehensive win. Pakistan had already secured their place in the semi-finals.

Ahmed Hussain starred with both bat and ball, scoring a brilliant 89 before claiming four wickets for 35 runs. Mohammad Sayyam and Mohammad Huzaifa picked up two wickets apiece to complete the victory.

Chasing 276, Nepal struggled to establish partnerships. Rohit Chand top-scored 37 off 54 balls, while opener Niraj Kumar Yadav contributed 29 from 59 deliveries. Suryanshu Koirala added 22, but Nepal failed to keep pace with the required run rate.

Abhay Yadav offered some late resistance with a quick-fire 23 off 16 balls, including three fours and a six, but the target remained beyond Nepal's reach.

Earlier, Pakistan recovered from early setback through a match-defining 135-run partnership between captain Farhan Yousaf and Ahmed Hussain.

After openers Usman Khan (19) and Jahangir Bilal (22) provided a 45-run start, Nepal fought back through Bipin Sharma and Sachin Bhatt, reducing Pakistan to 57-2. Bipin then dismissed Abdul Qadir for six, leaving the defending champions under pressure.

Farhan and Ahmed steadied the innings before accelerating to put Pakistan in control. Farhan scored 74 off 95 balls, hitting six fours and three sixes, while Ahmed produced an impressive 89 off 73 deliveries, including seven fours and two sixes.

Hasnain Abbas Dar added a useful 25 off 23 balls, helping Pakistan push their total to 275-7. Bipin was Nepal's leading bowler with three wickets for 58 runs.

With an unbeaten group-stage record and a semi-final place secured, Pakistan will now focus on defending their continental title.

Meanwhile in the same group India Under-19 secured a convincing 70-run victory over the United Arab Emirates to qualify for the last four.

Batting first, India posted 309-7, powered by Aaryavir Sehwag’s brilliant 160 off 168 balls and VK Vineeth’s 67. In reply, UAE managed 239 in 50 overs, with Ahmed Khudadad scoring 74. Ishan Sood starred with four wickets for India.

title: Nepal: Trishuli’s bustling bazar and a lifetime memories wiped out by disaster - Scroll.in
description: Nepal: Trishuli’s bustling bazar and a lifetime memories wiped out by disaster  Scroll.in
publisher.title: Scroll.in
full_article:
My father, Baa, and I stand on the debris of what used to be Trishuli Bazaar, Nuwakot, central Nepal. The expanse of the mud, rocks and silt spread before us, all the way down to the river. It is October and the river has now shrunk back to its regular autumn volume.

I put my arms around Baa to comfort him as he sighs.“Everything is gone,” there’s a catch in his voice.

Earlier this year, in March 2026, he had walked through Trishuli Bazaar, Nuwakot district in Nepal, entering shops, greeting passersby, shaking hands with past schoolmates, childhood friends and acquaintances. He had a spring in his step.

That was his first time back in over five decades since finishing high school and returning to his Kathmandu home to get on with adult life. My grandparents lived in Trishuli for 31 years when my grandmother was a staff nurse at Trishuli Hospital and my grandfather, a supervisor at the Trishuli Hydropower Station.

Baa would wonder why his parents abandoned the comfort of their Kathmandu life to move to Trishuli where they had to walk in scorching heat on hilly terrain to reach work, school, hospital, or the market. Settlements sprawling on the hills back the Trishuli Bazaar, overlooking the river it takes its name from. There’s a convergence of private homes, places of worship, businesses, and the hydropower station.

The Bhotekoshi flooding wiped out the main bazaar on 26 August 2026. Most of the settlements are gone.

Tents surrounded by devastation. Credit: Pratibha Tuladhar/Global Southasia.

The disaster, triggered by an earthquake in Tibet, led to a large-scale ice avalanche that caused glacial outburst, sending a river of debris towards Nepal’s Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers.

I was back in Trishuli last month. As of October 13, the death toll was over 1,450 and nearly 5,300 people were unaccounted for with 1.6 million people affected by the disaster, according to UNICEF’s Nepal humanitarian situation report .

Five months earlier, we had gathered over lunch around a big dining table at my great aunt, Nini-Aji’s home in Trishuli. The sound of the river, barely 30 metres from the house, was the background score.

My mother asked Nini-Aji if she ever felt scared to sleep, the river so close. Aji said she was so used to the sound; she misses it every time she is in Kathmandu.

“The river must come all the way up in monsoon?” my mother asked.

“It does but never all the way up.”

Credit: Pratibha Tuladhar/Global Southasia.

When we heard about the flood destroying Trishuli bazaar, our first concern was Nini-Aji, who is 86 and uses a walker. Several hours later we heard that her son and daughter-in-law had helped her crawl across a nettled wasteland before someone drove her to higher grounds.

She and many others were moved to Trishuli colony, built when the Trishuli Hydropower was being constructed with Indian aid in 1967.

My father and his siblings spent much of their childhood at the colony because of their parents’ jobs. As a child, I would be bussed off to Trishuli during winter holidays. It was warmer than Kathmandu. Days were slow.

Credit: Pratibha Tuladhar/Global Southasia.

The colony

My grandparents lived in the colony, in one of the semi-detached houses with a spacious front porch and a big backyard where they would grow vegetables and fruits – papaya, guava, sugarcane. In winter, we ate oranges and peanuts in the sun. A man with a turban carried a big dekchi (pot) on his head, selling snacks like khuwa and gundpakl. The rice came from fields nearby, as did the daal. There was enough fish from the river.

A musician who moonlighted as a supervisor at the hydro power station, my grandfather, would play his sitar in the drawing room in the evenings. Occasionally, a friend from the bazaar would join him on the tabla or other instrument and the house would reverberate with the melody of their jugalbandi.

Trishuli living was slow and sure and without distractions. I suppose that’s why my grandparents had chosen it over Kathmandu.

A man walks along the devastation by the Trishuli River. Credit: Pratibha Tuladhar/Global Southasia.

On every trip, I would carry loaves of bread from Kathmandu. Trishuli didn’t manufacture bread in the 80s. In return, they would pack my bag with all kinds of koseli (gifts) from Trishuli. At the bus stand at the bazaar, my father’s childhood friend, Khursheed Kaka, would run up to the bus window and hand me a bunch of bangles – he gifted me the prettiest bangles I ever wore.

Khursheed Kaka was no more when we visited in March, but we did meet some of Baa’s other Muslim-Newa schoolmates. When they opened their mouths to greet each other, they spoke Newa with an impeccable Kathmandu accent. We also ran into Pradeep uncle, who performs as the Lakhey, the masked demon, during the Janai Purnima festival. During the visit, there were other friends Baa sat with, holding hands, promising to come back for a longer visit, oblivious to the tragedy ahead.

A former trading post for Rasuwa and Dhading districts, Trishuli Bazaar had become a society comprising people from all backgrounds. The Ram Mandir, the high school, the mosque and the vihar were along the riverside, walking distance from each other. I was always surprised by how close they were to the river; one could just sprint towards the edge and dive.

I was always equally fascinated by how the residents of Trishuli Bazaar celebrated each other’s festivals together, joining Buddha Purnima processions and the jatras, and eating together during iftar.

At the Tribhuvan Trishuli High School, we talked to students at the hostel, who had come from far flung villages in Nuwakot and Rasuwa districts. We made several stops at houses by the river, meeting Baa’s and Nini’s former schoolmates. During my childhood visits, Nini sometimes took me to a video parlour in the bazaar, to watch a Hindi flick. Later, we would climb back to the colony, Nini singing songs from the film.

Aerial view of the damage left by flooding near Trishuli Bazar, Nuwakot, Nepal. Credit: Pratibha Tuladhar/Global Southasia.

Memories

For Baa, Trishuli is synonymous with so much. It was where he first saw mangoes growing on trees. It was where he bunked classes to go swimming and fishing in the river, where he first sat by the river professing his love to a school sweetheart, where he stole guavas with siblings and friends, where he heard his first ghost story, and where many nights, he held the torch and followed his mother to the homes of villagers in pain.

For me, it was a summation of the memories of my family members who had lived there.

On our trip in March, my mother marveled at how pretty and green Trishuli had become. It contrasted with her memories of the barren red clay hills rising above the colony, where she lived for a while as a newlywed. For a Kathmandu-bred, the sweltering hot climate only reminded her she was too far away from home. She missed her siblings; the bare red clay hills and the blinding thicket of trees around her were a reminder of her desolation.

Credit: Pratibha Tuladhar/Global Southasia.

But that image of Trishuli now changed for her. The denseness of trees in the colony had expanded to cover the bare hills nearby. All around Trishuli Bazaar, there were solid roads and nice hotels. The new bridge looked sturdy. There were mobile phone stores, marts and kitchenware. Some fancy dress stores catered to Rasuwa residents, displaying silken wanju-bakkhu and woollen kullu caps. The jewelry shops had some of the most intricate designs we ever saw.

After the floods, my mother talked about how she felt as if she had gone back only to impress upon her mind “a pretty picture of Trishuli before it was all wiped out.”

In March, as my brother drove us past the new Trishuli bridge, I craned my head to look at the river, feeling squeamish. I have always felt a deep sense of fear near roaring rivers, like the sound comes bearing premonition.

In 2012, my mentor, DJ Clark and I had followed Pradeep Mool, a specialist at ICIMOD, the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, to the China-Nepal border in Rasuwa for a story ( The River that Rages ) about imminent GLOFs, glacial lake outburst floods.

The warning about potential damage left my hands clammy as I interviewed Tamang residents along the border. The region had seen flash floods in the past and resettled – as though awaiting another cycle of disaster, then recovery.

Play

A few years later, fellow journalist Rajneesh Bandari and I had followed the route again to work on another story on GLOFs. Ishwar Shrestha, a hotel owner in Bahrabise, Rasuwa, had asked if flash floods were real. Even if they were, he said, he would never be able to abandon his home because where would he go?

When we awoke to the horrific news of Bhotekoshi flooding in August, it was Ishwar Shrestha who first came to mind. Many in the region might have shared his sentiment as they fled their homes that day. And many found it hard to leave homes they had built with their lifetime’s savings.

A house means everything in weather conditions that are harsh and in an economy that has little to offer the poor. Therefore, many return, build at the very spot of disaster because there is nowhere else they can afford to build. There’s only so much to abandon, as well as to return to.

Credit: Pratibha Tuladhar/Global Southasia.

From the moment the Bhotekoshi disaster struck, Baa was glued to his phone, trying to contact relatives and childhood friends. Phones were down and updates were sketchy. He managed to speak to just one: Dhruba Shrestha Uncle, who limps from a road accident injury and needs assistance walking. In March, Baa and he sat at his little shop near Tribhuvan Trishuli High School, their hands gently resting on each other’s knees, conversing, planning another meeting.

In August, his son helped Dhruba Uncle evacuate to Trishuli colony from the bazaar as the flood filth surged. His wife, halfway during fleeing, decided to run back to the house in a moment of frenzy to bring the five lakh rupees in cash they had been saving for their son’s wedding.

“We couldn’t find my wife,” Dhruba’s uncle told Baa. “She and the house are gone. There’s nothing to say. We are without an address.”

The aftermath

During our October visit, Baa stands at a distance and watches me speak to Buddha Maya Tamang – a 13-year-old whose sister was swept away along with their home in Betrawati, Nuwakot. She and others who were displaced have been relocated to nearby government schools. But the new life comes with the challenge of navigating memories of the one they were forced to leave behind.

UNICEF figures estimate that over 32,000 children are impacted by the floods. Many of them are living in holding centres. Some who were orphaned have moved in with relatives. For many, it’s a long wait before they can be housed with a family.

“I used to like the thought of becoming a teacher, but right now, I don’t know,” Buddha Maya says.

“She used to be a bubbly child, but has changed completely since the flood,” explains Sabitri Magar, a school assistant, who has known Buddha Maya since she was in kindergarten.

Since nature changed its course after the flood, Trishuli river flows at the threshold of Sabitri’s home in Betrawati. They can no longer live there. The family had earlier moved to Betrawati from Katichap after being displaced by a landslide: “It’s like we are being stalked by disasters.”

Sabitri currently lives with her four children in a rented room in Batar. But rents have doubled since the flood with the influx of homeless people. In some places in Nuwakot, the displaced live in tents. As the winter sets in, they will have to find warmer accommodation.

Many are so desperate that they have started cleaning up their old homes to try and move back in, even though these flood-ravaged homes are not safe. As with all disasters, relief distribution has not always been fair. There are challenges of language, reach, access to authority and the displaced persons’ inability to articulate.

“People have received enough dry food and clothes in donation now and that’s not even the need anymore,” says Bhawani Panta, school teacher. “What people need is money to buy medicines and other essentials. Most of all, they need homes. Those in authority need to hurry up.”

Pratibha Tuladhar worked for nearly 14 years with Kantipur Television. She recently traveled back to Trishuli, a town destroyed by the floods in Nepal. A shorter version of this piece was first published by Nepali Times , where she currently writes a column.
